title: The du'a of Ta'if
hook: in an orchard outside Ta'if he prays: to You I complain of my weakness; if You are not angry with me, I don't mind (sirah)
carry: if you're not angry, I don't mind

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ta'if: three brothers said no, a crowd drove him out, and he kept walking. Your line was: he walked on.

The crowd has fallen back. He's sitting in the shade of a vine, against the wall of an orchard that belongs to two men of Quraysh. Refused by three leaders, jeered at by a town, he has nowhere obvious to go next. What would anyone say, alone, in a moment like that? A complaint about the people of Ta'if would make sense. So would a plea to be avenged. Ibn Ishaq records something else. Today: du'a.
screen: `IN THE SHADE OF A VINE.` → `NOWHERE TO GO.` → `WHAT DOES HE SAY?`

segments.voice: A du'a is a personal prayer, words addressed to Allah in a person's own need, as opposed to the set prayer, the salah. This one, as Ibn Ishaq gives it, begins with a complaint, but not against Thaqif. He complains to Allah of his own weakness: his lack of strength, his lack of means, how small he has become in people's eyes. Then he turns. He calls Allah the most merciful of the merciful, the Lord of the weak, and asks: to whom are You leaving me? To a stranger who will scowl at me, or an enemy given power over me? And then comes today's line. If You are not angry with me, he says, I don't mind. Your well-being, the ease You give, is wider for me. Look at the order. First, honesty: I am weak, I have little, people look down on me. Then a question, almost a child's: who are You handing me to? Only then the turn, which isn't that the pain stops mattering, but that it's measured against one thing. If the relationship with Allah is whole, the rest can be borne. Notice what is missing, too: no curse on Ta'if, no request that the town be punished. That restraint will matter in two days. A note on the source: this du'a comes from the sirah, through Ibn Ishaq, not from Bukhari or Muslim, and hadith scholars have discussed the strength of its chain. Its words are still said today, in hard times.
screen: `A DU'A: A PRAYER IN ONE'S OWN NEED.` · `FIRST: I AM WEAK.` · `TO WHOM ARE YOU LEAVING ME?` · `NO CURSE ON TA'IF.` · then, large: `IF YOU ARE NOT ANGRY, I DON'T MIND.`

segments.voice: Sit with your hands open in your lap, and silently name three honest things: where your strength has run low, where you don't have what you need, where you feel small in other people's eyes. If you pray, you can bring them to Allah in your own words, as plainly as he did, or in the words of the du'a of Ta'if if you know them. If you don't pray, notice what it's like to say them without defending yourself.
Du'a, a personal prayer. In an orchard after rejection, he complains to Allah of his own weakness and says: if You are not angry with me, I don't mind. Today's word.
Your line: if you're not angry, I don't mind. Honest about weakness, and still turned toward Allah. That's day seven hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: The du'a of Ta'if is taught in sirah study alongside the journey to Ta'if, and Muslims say its words in times of hardship or rejection.

chat.says: What did the Prophet pray after Ta'if drove him out?
options: He named his weakness and said: if You're not angry with me, I don't mind.
He asked Allah to punish Ta'if for how its people treated him.
He prayed for an army to come back and take the town for Islam.
chat.meaning: In Ibn Ishaq's telling he complains of his own weakness, not of Thaqif, and says: if You are not angry with me, I don't mind.

notes: The du'a is paraphrased throughout; no translation is quoted (Guillaume 1955 is under copyright). Confirm the paraphrase is faithful, especially 'Your protection is wider for me'.
The script states hadith scholars 'have discussed the strength of its chain' without naming a grading; a Keeper may want to name the grading or soften further.
'Its words are still said today' is kept general on purpose under the claims rule.
The practice invites saying the du'a's own words only if the listener already knows them; no new prayer is written.
The orchard owners (Utba and Shayba, sons of Rabi'a) are referred to as 'two men of Quraysh'; they are named tomorrow.
